title: Elizabeth of Hungary
hookLine: a young noblewoman who spent her fortune on a hospital; legend says bread turned to roses

cards: A young woman hurries down from a castle with her cloak held closed. Underneath is bread, a lot of it, for the hungry people waiting below.

Someone stops her on the path; in some tellings it's her husband, in others a suspicious relative. What are you carrying? She can't hide it, so she opens the cloak, and what falls out, the legend says, is roses.
That's the story people tell about Elizabeth of Hungary, a king's daughter who married into a noble German house. The roses are a legend. The bread is not.

teach.h: A KING'S DAUGHTER AT A GERMAN COURT.
teach.b: Elizabeth was born to Hungary's royal family and sent as a girl to the court of Thuringia, in Germany, to marry Louis, the son of its ruler, who later ruled there himself.
The early accounts say the marriage was a loving one. They also say she wasn't a comfortable person to have at a royal table. She refused food she believed had been taken unjustly from the poor.

teach.h: SHE WENT DOWN TO THE SICK.
teach.b: In a time of hunger she gave out grain from the stores, and she went down to the sick herself. Then her husband died, away from home, on his way to a crusade, and her life changed fast.
She left court and took up a life of poverty, close to the Franciscans.
With what was left of her fortune she built a hospital at Marburg, and worked in it: washing, feeding, sitting with people others avoided. Behind this is a passage in Matthew.
When the Son of man comes in his glory, the king tells people, "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." Whatever they did for the least of his family, they did for him.
In the Gospel's own terms, feeding the hungry is serving Christ. In the Gospels' Greek, bread is artos, the same word as in the prayer, give us this day our daily bread. And the roses?
Some hear a miracle, some a picture: what you give in secret becomes beautiful. Either way, the story keeps her as she was, caught on the path, holding bread for someone else.

how: Catholics, Lutherans and Anglicans honor Elizabeth of Hungary, and among hospitals, charities and parishes named for her, some of them mark her feast day with bread or food for the poor.

games.q: you're Elizabeth, carrying bread under your cloak. someone stops you on the path and asks what you're carrying. what do you do?
o: say it's nothing and keep walking.
games.why: in the legend she opens the cloak, and roses fall out. in the history, the bread kept coming.

practice: Think of someone who could use bread this week, in any form: a sick neighbor, a coworker who skips lunch, a shelter or food bank near you. Let one face or place come, and picture bringing it, nothing hidden.
If you pray, hold that person in prayer; if not, hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Elizabeth. A king's daughter of Hungary who fed the hungry, served the sick at a hospital she built, and, legend says, carried bread that became roses.
